Radar cross section (RCS) is a measure of an object's detectability by radar and depends on shape, size, and material.
Shaping and radar absorbing materials (RAM) are traditional passive methods for RCS reduction.
RAM works by absorbing incident radar energy and converting it into heat, reducing reflected signals.
Metamaterials are engineered composites with electromagnetic properties not found in natural materials, such as negative permittivity and permeability.
Negative Index Metamaterials (NIM) have simultaneous negative permittivity and permeability, resulting in a negative refractive index.
Frequency Selective Surfaces (FSS) are periodic arrays that filter electromagnetic waves by frequency, enabling control over radar wave reflection and transmission.
Active cancellation emits signals that destructively interfere with radar echoes to reduce RCS but requires precise timing and phase control.
Microstrip patch antennas have high RCS but can be modified using metamaterials to reduce radar visibility while improving antenna performance.
The proposed metamaterial unit cell consists of a square loop and intersecting strips at the edges of the antenna ground plane.
Radar detection range depends on the fourth root of the RCS; halving detection range requires a 16-fold RCS reduction.
Electromagnetic Bandgap (EBG) metamaterials prohibit wave propagation in certain frequency bands, aiding in RCS reduction.
Chiral metamaterials have non-zero chirality parameter and affect circularly polarized waves, useful in stealth applications.
RAM coatings are often toxic and require uniform application to be effective.
Modern radar systems operate across a wide frequency range from VHF (30–300 MHz) to Ka-band (27–40 GHz).
Passive cancellation involves adjusting phase and amplitude of scattered waves to cancel radar reflections locally.
Metamaterials enable antenna miniaturization, bandwidth expansion, and gain enhancement alongside RCS reduction.
Active cancellation is most effective at low radar frequencies where scattering lobes are broad.
Shaping techniques must balance aerodynamic requirements with RCS reduction goals.
Composite AMC (Artificial Magnetic Conductor) surfaces can be designed to achieve broadband RCS reduction.
The paper reviews recent research on metamaterial-based RCSR and proposes new unit cell designs for stealth applications.
